Then shall be seated another katun = Three: are his breads: three are his waters: Jicama <note>cup, a root crop used as famine food</note>: is his bread: jicama: is his water: this he takes for his meal: this he drinks = X batun = the chichim plant: chaya: he takes for his meal = this was seated: here in the town of misery, O Father: within the Bolon tun = in the time when there are: foreigners = bearing the burden of the katun: at the end of its years = Ox la hun ahau = then he set down his foot: - Buluc ahau = then descended the word: of Bo lon ɔa cab = the tip of his tongue = Then descended: the halting, of the burden of the katun: the katun = Nine is its burden: Then it descended: from heaven = yellow was the day: when was bound = its burden: there: Then descended water: coming from the midst of the heart of heaven = so that might be reborn: Bolon haaban: his house: and with it descended: Bolon mayel: sweet rain <note>cha huc, thunder shower or sweet rain</note>:

<summary>This page continues the prophetic narrative of the Chilam Balam of Chumayel, completing the installation of Kan tenel ahau and detailing the hardships, riddles, and famine foods associated with the katun cycle of Ox ahau. <meta>continues from previous page: the plumeria flower corruption passage</meta>Greedy is his mouth. Insolent is his word in his rule, in the time of the breaking of bread = in the time of understanding: his throat. With the corners of his mouth he eats, behind his claws he takes his food; his mouth is neither wood nor stone. Great is his madness at Lahun Chan. As for his face where he sits: sinful is his face, sinful is his word, sinful is his speech, sinful is his understanding, sinful is his walk. Bandaged are his eyes where he sits; a red settlement is his mat. He sits in the midst of his rule, in the heap of his father, in the heap of his mother; nor does he know his mother. Quickly kindled is his heart by lust. Among the fatherless, those greedy for a father, among the motherless he shall walk; drunken is his spirit, lost is his understanding beside his father, beside his mother. There is no reverence in him, there is no goodness in his heart; only on the tip of his tongue is there a little boiling. He does not know how it shall come to an end, nor does he know what is at the end of his rule. That is when the time of his reign shall come to an end.

<note>A pen flourish marks the end of the paragraph.</note>

Here is Bolon ti ku: Bolon Chan, the face of the lordly men, he of the two-day mat, he of the two-day throne. This one came within the Ox Ahau katun, and there shall be another lord of the province <note>Maya: "peten", referring to the island or region of Yucatan</note>, the establisher of the word of another katun, when the word of the Ox Ahau katun shall come to an end in the time of the selling of sons. This shall be over the stammerers, the Itza: one bread of Chuen, one bread; there shall be ground up one single stone of the loincloth of the sin of the stammerers, the Itza. This is Bolon ti ku. This shall be the ending of the word of the Ox Ahau katun, and the coming of understanding to the rulership of the towns. At the ending of the word of the katun, then shall be made manifest the lineage of the noble-born, the <term>Batabob</term> <gloss>town governors</gloss>, and the other prudent men, and the lineage of the Batabob who had earth stamped secretly into their faces, when they were made as nothing by the mad sun, the mad katun.

<summary>This page continues the prophetic condemnation of corrupt rulers from the Chilam Balam of Chumayel, describing their greed, blindness, and loss of reverence before their reign ends. It then prophesies the close of the Ox Ahau katun under Bolon ti ku, foretelling the judgment of the Itza and the eventual restoration of the true lineage of the noble-born and town governors after a period of madness and humiliation.</summary>
<keywords>Chilam Balam of Chumayel, Lahun Chan, Bolon ti ku, Bolon Chan, Ox Ahau katun, Itza, Batabob, prophecy, kingship, noble lineage</keywords>

Ji Xianian listened without answering. He merely said, "Never mind that. He is not at home today. I will just tell him to go tomorrow."

The following day, Ji Xianian walked to the gate of the Shi residence at Lower Floating Bridge. When he tried to enter, the gatekeeper stopped him, saying, "Who are you, barging inside like this?"

Ji Xianian said, "I am here to write calligraphy."

The young servant came out from the porter's lodge, caught sight of him, and said, "So it is you! You can write calligraphy too?"

After this furious shouting and scolding, Squire Shi was left speechless, hanging his head as he retreated inside. Ji Xianian shouted some more abuse for a while, then went back to the Tianjie Monastery as before.

There was another man who sold paper spill tubes <note>paper tightly rolled to transfer flame, used especially for lighting pipes</note>. His surname was Wang and his given name was Tai. For generations his family had sold vegetables at Sanpailou. By his father's time, the family had fallen into poverty and sold off all their vegetable plots. From early childhood, Wang Tai loved playing <term>weiqi</term> <gloss>Go, the traditional board game of encircling territory</gloss> best of all. Later, after his father died, he had no means of making a living, so every day he went to the Hujuguan area to sell paper spills for his livelihood. 

One day, a temple fair was held at Miaoyi Nunnery. That nunnery faced Wulong Pool. It was just the beginning of summer, and the pool was crowded with fresh green lotus leaves.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and it is Spirit. The sages also worried that while the principle emerges through images and numbers, the verbal pronouncements of hexagrams and lines cannot encompass it entirely. Thus they once remarked by way of contrast, saying: "Spirit has no localized direction, and the *Changes* has no fixed physical form." They also said: "One yin and one yang is what is called the Way." 

Now, whatever has a localized direction and a physical form is a concrete object. Even Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, are concrete objects. Yet the function does not separate from concrete objects, and its efficacy transcends the realm of physical things. Therefore, that which subtly animates the ten thousand things without being fathomable is Spirit. It sets into motion thunder, wind, water, and fire, silently gathering the functions of movement, swaying, drying, and moistening. For this reason, the six children <note>the six derivative trigrams representing natural elements</note> are put to service under Qian and Kun <note>Heaven and Earth, the two primary hexagrams</note>. When the *Shuogua* <gloss>Discussion of the Trigrams</gloss> commentary speaks of subtly animating things, it does not include Heaven and Earth in the list of the six physical entities. 

Therefore, service takes the One as master, and considers Spirit to be the ultimate. Outstanding is the discourse on the One by Meng Jingyi <note>Meng Yi, a fourth-century Jin dynasty scholar</note> of the Jin period: "The wonder of the One lies in its mysterious void transcending the boundary of concrete existence, while its spiritual transformations abundantly supply endless generation. Acting as

<summary>Cheng Dachang explains that Spirit and the Way transcend physical form while functioning through concrete things, harmonizing the hexagrams and trigram functions. He introduces Meng Jingyi's Jin-era discourse to elucidate how the mysterious One governs all transformations without being confined by physical reality.</summary>
<keywords>Cheng Dachang, Book of Changes, Yijing, Spirit, Shen, Dao, Way, Qian, Kun, Shuogua, Discussion of the Trigrams, six children trigrams, Meng Jingyi, Jin dynasty, the One</keywords>

Applying this statement to the *Changes*, the Supreme Ultimate <term>Taiji</term> <gloss>Supreme Ultimate</gloss> encompasses the myriad things, and its guiding principle can thus be sought."

### V. The *Changes* takes the One as ancestor and Spirit as the ultimate

The One emerges from the void to produce the concrete: this is the Supreme Ultimate generating the ten thousand things. Spirit accumulates the concrete to transform into the void: this achieves unfathomable efficacy through a measurable accumulation. Therefore, it is spoken of as subtly animating the ten thousand things. Changes and transformations operate in the unseen realm, truly difficult to exhaust in speech. Yet if the principles of the hexagrams and lines do not reach human nature, destiny, and human affairs, then the *Changes* becomes useless. Thereupon, by borrowing the visible realm of human affairs to deduce the invisible realm of Heaven and Earth, their categories and kinds correspond with each other. For before joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure are aroused, the One is not yet

<summary>Cheng Dachang continues citing Meng Jingyi on how the transcendent One encompasses the myriad things, then asserts that the Book of Changes takes the One as origin and Spirit as ultimate. He argues that hexagram principles must connect with human affairs and psychological states to illuminate the unseen workings of Heaven and Earth.</summary>

Once aroused, joy opposes anger, and sorrow opposes pleasure. Extending this by analogy, where there is benevolence there is righteousness; where there is ritual propriety there is music; where there is above there is below; where there is right there is wrong. In all such cases, that which was formerly the One emerges and divides into two.

From duality onward, as traces become ever more numerous, departure from the One becomes ever more distant. Therefore, from the two central qualities of trustworthiness and goodness down to beauty and greatness <note>referencing Mencius 7B:25, which outlines stages of spiritual development: being desirable is good, having it in oneself is true/trustworthy, being full is beautiful, being full and having great radiance is great, and being great and transformed is holy/sage-like</note>, one accumulates upward, seeking in every step to attain spiritual transformation. If one attains this state, all disparate traces gather together and return to their beginning. 

When this primal application is reached, gathering without scattering, then the One becomes the present reality. Once unified, trustworthiness, goodness, beauty, and greatness leave no visible traces, yet one responds to every stimulus as it arises. Here lies the emblem of the One being able to generate the myriad things. When confronting a situation requiring benevolence, one acts with benevolence; when desiring righteousness, one acts with righteousness; when encountering ritual propriety or wisdom, ritual propriety and wisdom come forth, without anyone observing any forced effort.

<summary>Cheng Dachang explains how the unified Supreme Ultimate divides into polar dualities upon emotional and moral arousal, moving outward into numerous visible traces. By ascending through the stages of moral cultivation toward spiritual transformation, one gathers these dispersed expressions back into the primal One, enabling effortless and spontaneous moral responsiveness to all things.</summary>

The Commentary on the Attached Verbalizations <note>original: "繫辭", the <term>Xici</term>, also known as the Great Treatise of the <term>Yijing</term></note> states: 

Heaven is exalted and Earth is lowly, and thus <term>Qian</term> <gloss>Creative/Heaven</gloss> and <term>Kun</term> <gloss>Receptive/Earth</gloss> are determined. The low and the high are arrayed, and thus the noble and the base assume their stations. Movement and rest have their regularities, and thus the firm and the yielding are distinguished. Directions gather according to their kind, and things divide according to their classes; thus good fortune and misfortune arise. In heaven forms become celestial images; on earth they become physical shapes. Thus change and transformation become visible. Therefore the firm and the yielding rub against one another, and the eight trigrams resonate and displace one another. They are stirred by thunder and lightning, and nourished by wind and rain. The sun and moon course in their orbits; one cold season yields to one warm season. The Way of Qian establishes the male; the Way of Kun establishes the female.

The <term>Zhouyi</term> <gloss>Book of Changes of Zhou</gloss> operates through structural inversion and opposition <note>original: "反對", referring to paired hexagrams formed either by turning a hexagram upside down or by inverting all its yin and yang lines</note>. The Commentary on the Attached Verbalizations is affixed to King Wen's <term>Zhouyi</term>. Therefore, in this opening chapter of the Attached Verbalizations, the Master <note>Confucius</note> illuminates the principle of structural inversion and opposition. In the Pre-Heaven <note>Earlier Heaven arrangement attributed to Fuxi</note>, there are eight trigrams; in the Post-Heaven <note>Later Heaven arrangement attributed to King Wen</note>, structural inversion reduces them to six. In the Pre-Heaven, there are sixty-four hexagrams; in the Post-Heaven, structural inversion reduces them to thirty-six. The sixty-four...

<summary>This page quotes the opening chapter of the Xici (Great Treatise) to demonstrate how the dual cosmological forces of Qian and Kun govern change. It then explains how King Wen's Later Heaven sequence utilizes the principle of hexagram inversion and opposition, reducing the sixty-four distinct hexagrams into thirty-six operational pairs.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>are the expansion of eight; the thirty-six are the expansion of six. Therefore, the Commentary on the Attached Verbalizations <note>original: "繫辭", <term>Xici</term></note> says: "Heaven is exalted and Earth is lowly, and thus <term>Qian</term> <gloss>Creative/Heaven</gloss> and <term>Kun</term> <gloss>Receptive/Earth</gloss> are determined." This refers to how the Upper Classic begins with Qian and Kun. It further says: "They are stirred by thunder and lightning, and nourished by wind and rain." This refers to how the Lower Classic begins with <term>Zhen</term> <gloss>Thunder</gloss>, <term>Gen</term> <gloss>Mountain</gloss>, <term>Xun</term> <gloss>Wind</gloss>, and <term>Dui</term> <gloss>Lake</gloss>. It says: "The sun and moon course in their orbits; one cold season yields to one warm season." Here, <term>Kan</term> <gloss>Water</gloss> and <term>Li</term> <gloss>Fire</gloss> function as the operational dynamic of both the Upper and Lower Classics. 

Its speaking of thunder and lightning without mentioning Gen differs from the Discussion of the Trigrams <note>original: "說卦", <term>Shuogua</term></note>, which pairs thunder and wind; this is precisely to illuminate the structural inversion and opposition between Zhen and Gen. Its speaking of wind and rain without mentioning Dui differs from the Discussion of the Trigrams, which pairs mountain and lake; this is precisely to illuminate the structural inversion and opposition between Xun and Dui. Gen is not explicitly mentioned because Gen is already implicit within Zhen; Dui is not explicitly mentioned because Dui is already implicit within Xun. In this way, the eight-by-eight structural opposition of the <term>Lianshan</term> <gloss>Mountains in Succession</gloss> system of changes becomes the principle of six-by-six pairs in the <term>Zhouyi</term>.

<summary>This page analyzes the structural design of the Upper and Lower Classics of the Zhouyi, showing how selective mentions of trigram pairs in the Xici demonstrate the principle of structural inversion between hexagrams. It explains how this structural pairing transforms the earlier eightfold Lianshan system into the thirty-six paired hexagrams of the Zhouyi.</summary>
